title: My body and privacy
subject: RSHE

thread_tags.line: Thread tags: SMSC S/M/So (C: none); British Values IL/MR (D/RL/T: none).
thread_tags.rationale: S: consider a fictional person’s dignity and choices. M: distinguish respectful actions from pressure or intrusion. So: listen and respond to another person’s boundary. IL: respect a choice to pause or use an aid. MR: respect privacy, personal space and a refusal. No other thread is claimed.

label: Public edition
objective_verbatim: Use accurate taught body-part words and recognise a basic privacy rule.
display_objective: Use taught body words. Choose an act that gives privacy.
approved_activity: Use clear, age-appropriate body diagrams to match or identify the taught words.
Sort fictional privacy situations and choose a respectful action, including asking for help when unsure.
calendar_note: Year A. 16–20 November 2026. One 40-minute lesson. No day or clock slot inferred. Week 7 is assessing.
where_this_leads: This helps me respect privacy and dignity in shared spaces.
unit: Body privacy, personal space and permission
accreditation: The qualification and the accredited unit: staff confirm any mapping from actual work. No criteria or completion are inferred.
assessment: Weeks 1–6 are formative. Week 7 is the assessing lesson. Keep actual responses, support, gaps and next steps in the evidence record.

sources.note: The owner-approved standalone RSHE outline is the weekly teaching source. The three build notes apply throughout. No separate workbook row is asserted.

authoring_provenance.note: Newly authored tasks from the owner-approved RSHE outline. No separate workbook row is asserted. All people and situations are fictional. Accurate anatomical terms and everyday permission principles were checked against primary guidance.

external_sources.note: Approval, curriculum context, template and authored visual provenance.

evidence.description: An individual vocabulary response and two privacy decisions, with support recorded.
evidence.status: not prefilled; actual response and support to be recorded

routes.Supported: Supported: match one taught word using two choices, then choose a respectful action for two different privacy stories with reading or scribing support.
routes.Independent: Independent: identify the four taught words on the diagram and record two privacy decisions with reasons from the stories.
routes.Aspire: Aspire: explain why seeking help does not break a privacy rule, and distinguish necessary care from a secret request; retain the core vocabulary response and two decisions.

vocab.definition: A body part at the front, above the scrotum.
The skin sac that holds the testicles.
Body parts held inside the scrotum.
The genital parts on the outside of the body.
Space to do a task in private.
Treat a person and their choices with care.
Support with a worry or a need.

cases.text: A young person is changing clothes. Another person knocks and waits outside.
cases.next_step: Wait outside for a reply; do not assume permission to enter.

cases.text: A young person is using a toilet. Someone opens the closed door without asking.
cases.next_step: Close the door, give privacy and wait. Use agreed urgent-help arrangements if there is a genuine safety concern.

cases.text: A young person has a worry about a private body part. They tell a trusted adult.
cases.next_step: The adult listens and arranges appropriate help. Talking about a worry is not breaking a privacy rule.

cases.text: Someone asks a young person to show a part under their pants and keep it secret.
cases.judgement: Seek help. The request is not okay.
cases.next_step: The young person can move away if able and tell a trusted adult. If the first adult does not help, tell another. They are never to blame for someone else’s harmful action.

cases.text: A young person needs help to wash. A care adult explains the help, asks first and gives privacy.
cases.next_step: Follow the agreed care plan, explain each step, seek and respond to the person’s wishes and provide only the help needed. An adult’s role alone is not permission.

cases.text: A young person asks for help with a worry. The first adult is busy.
cases.judgement: A further help route is needed.
cases.next_step: The young person can tell another trusted adult and keep seeking help. Do not treat a delayed response as proof that the worry is unimportant.

A respects privacy in this fictional situation. B and C do not. Privacy protects dignity; it must never mean keeping a worry or harmful act secret. Reteach with the closed-door story and the help-seeking story. In urgent care or danger, staff follow the setting’s agreed procedure, explain what is happening and protect dignity as far as possible.

Supported: match one taught word using two choices, then choose a respectful action for two different privacy stories with reading or scribing support. Independent: identify the four taught words on the diagram and record two privacy decisions with reasons from the stories. Aspire: explain why seeking help does not break a privacy rule, and distinguish necessary care from a secret request; retain the core vocabulary response and two decisions.

Use four minutes to match or identify taught words on the supplied diagram. Use five minutes to sort fictional privacy situations and record decisions for two different cards, normally A and B. Use three minutes to consider C or D and name a help route. Preserve the first response, prompts and any change. A learner may pass; record the gap and offer a supported follow-up.
Read aloud, point, scribe exact words or use the usual communication aid. Record support without treating speech speed or handwriting as the target.

All teaching prompts concern fictional young people. Never ask about a learner’s own body, family or experiences. Use only the supplied diagrams and stories. No body checking, touching, removing clothes, photographs, real-life comparisons or personal role-play. An adult may read both parts of a fictional exchange; learners can choose or describe a response. Respect a pass, pause or quiet response without asking why. Follow the setting’s safeguarding procedure if a personal concern arises; do not turn a disclosure into lesson evidence. Use the agreed support and care arrangements.

Keep the exact taught word list and the learner’s word-to-diagram response, including any point or selected card. Keep decisions for two distinct fictional privacy stories with the action chosen; record reasons where offered, actual support and what remains unshown. Reading aloud or pointing is valid. No real body, private history or disclosure belongs in the lesson evidence record.

Use VF · WS · I · NS+ (Yellow Box) · // self-edit · ? read back · R responded · E evidence in the evidence record. R requires Voice, Audience, a specific NS+ prompt and the learner response in their own colour. E is recorded only when actual work is banked. Record prompts and unfinished work. Blank sheets and adult models are not completed learner evidence.

Space: calm seating and clear resources. Voice: an optional response about the fictional case. Audience: an adult listens or reads and responds. Influence: record any change to the task support or next teaching step. A pass is respected and does not require an explanation.

S: consider a fictional person’s dignity and choices. M: distinguish respectful actions from pressure or intrusion. So: listen and respond to another person’s boundary. IL: respect a choice to pause or use an aid. MR: respect privacy, personal space and a refusal. No other thread is claimed.

A response about a fictional privacy decision or help route may be offered to the Communication portfolio. Record the learner’s actual chosen or spoken response and the adult’s reply. Staff decide any mapping.

Staff may substitute the setting’s own taught list. Use plain anatomical terms and an accurate matching diagram, and record the words actually taught. This issue teaches penis, scrotum, testicles and vulva. The dotted ovals show testicles inside the scrotum; they are not visible through the skin. The vulva label covers the outside genital parts, not an internal organ. Do not link the diagrams to a real person or ask learners which diagram resembles them.

Private body parts are not dirty or shameful. Privacy is not an instruction to keep harmful behaviour secret. A trusted adult can help with a body worry. The vulva is the external group of genital parts; it is not the internal vagina. The scrotum is the skin sac, while the testicles are inside it. The diagram is simplified and not a standard against which to judge any body.
